rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orchard owner represents the hypocrite or show-off whose deeds God has erased; he discovers the loss when old, helpless, and responsible for young dependents.
rows.anchor: هذا مثل ضربه الله، تبارك وتعالى، للمنافقين والمرائين بأعمالهم لا يريدونه بشيء منها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others give this as the meaning: the man loses his fruitful orchard precisely when age, weakness, and dependent children make him need it most.
rows.anchor: وهو معنى قول ابن عباس وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier smooth-stone parable likewise depicts God erasing show-offs’ earnings, leaving them unable to draw on them when they need them.
rows.anchor: يريد سبحانه: أنه محق كسبهم، فلم يقدروا عليه حين حاجتهم إليه، كما أذهب المطر التراب عن الصفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He glosses تثبيتا من أنفسهم as confirmation made real from within themselves.
rows.anchor: أي: تحقيقا من أنفسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A garden on an elevated place is especially fruitful, since gardens and orchards are at their best on heights.
rows.anchor: وأحسن ما تكون الجنان والرياض: على الربا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: وابل means the heaviest rain, which makes the garden yield twice its usual produce.
rows.anchor: أصابها وابل وهو: أشد المطر، فأضعفت في الحمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: طل is lighter rain; even with it the garden’s fruit yield is not diminished from what it would be with heavy rain.
rows.anchor: وهو: أضعف المطر. فتلك حالها في النزل وتضاعف الثمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sleep may be called sabāt because it involves stretching out; an unattributed poetic fragment precedes this lexical observation.
rows.anchor: ثم قد يسمى النوم سباتا، لأنه بالتمدد يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise’s vessels and furnishings differ from human-made things here; God uses familiar present things to indicate unseen realities.
rows.anchor: كل ما في الجنة من آلتها وسررها وفرشها وأكوابها- مخالف لما في الدنيا من صنعة العباد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says that the things of Paradise have nothing in common with this world except their names.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: ليس في الدنيا شيء مما في الجنة إلا الأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Akwaab are cups without handles; earthly cups can be made of either silver or glass.
rows.anchor: والأكواب: كيزان لا عرى لها، وهي في الدنيا قد تكون من فضة، وتكون من قوارير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording compares Paradise glass to silver: its cups combine silver’s whiteness with glass’s clarity, like calling a drink ‘light’.
rows.anchor: أراد قوارير كأنها من فضة، كما تقول: أتانا بشراب من نور، أي كأنه نور

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains the comparison as the women’s clarity like ruby and whiteness like coral.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة في قول الله عز وجل:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the stones of clay as baked bricks, hard like stone.
rows.anchor: فإن ابن عباس، رضي الله عنه، ذكر أنها آجر. والآجر: حجارة الطين، لأنه في صلابة الحجارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba says he read in the Torah that Noah’s descendants settled at Saeer and burned bricks into stone while building a tower toward heaven.
rows.anchor: وقرأت في التوراة بعد ذكر أنساب ولد نوح صلى الله عليه وسلم: أنهم تفرقوا في كل أرض

rows.speaker: بعض من رأى هذه الحجارة
rows.claim: Some who saw the stones described them as red and stamped.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعض من رأى هذه الحجارة أنها حمر مختمة

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others described the stones as striped, which Ibn Qutayba connects with their being marked.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: مخططة، وذلك تسويمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some explain سجّيل through Persian sang and gil, meaning stone and clay.
rows.anchor: ولهذا ذهب قوم في تفسير (سجيل) إلى سنك وكل. أي حجر وطين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although addressed to the Messenger, the verse means other doubters, since Arabs may address one person while intending another.
rows.anchor: فإن المخاطبة لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، والمراد غيره من الشكاك

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators take ذي ظفر as every bird with a claw and every livestock animal with a hoof; calling a hoof a nail is metaphorical.
rows.anchor: أي كل ذي مخلب من الطير، وكل ذي حافر من الدواب كذلك قال المفسرون

rows.speaker: الشاعر الآخر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet uses حافر for a foot, supporting the metaphorical naming of a hoof as a nail.
rows.anchor: كما قال الآخر وذكر ضيفا طرقه :

rows.speaker: الشاعر الآخر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet calls feet أظلاف, although that word properly belongs to sheep and cattle hooves.
rows.anchor:
وقال آخر :
سأمنعها أو سوف أجعل أمرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab idiom calls a man غليظ المشافر, meaning thick-lipped, although مشافر properly names camel lips.
rows.anchor: والعرب تقول للرجل: (هو غليظ المشافر) تريد الشفتين، والمشافر للإبل

rows.speaker: الحطيئة
rows.claim: Al-Hutayʾa’s use of مشافره for a man’s lips witnesses the camel-word’s metaphorical extension.
rows.anchor:
وقال الحطيئة :
قروا جارك العيمان لما جفوته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses باليمين as by strength, since the strength of anything lies in its right side.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: اليمين هاهنا: القوة. وإنما أقام اليمين مقام القوة، لأن قوة كل شيء في ميامنه

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Another linguistic interpretation takes it as seizing someone by the hand, an idiom for taking hold of and punishing him.
rows.anchor: ولأهل اللغة في هذا مذهب آخر قد جرى الناس على اعتياده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba favors the idiomatic punishment sense: if the Messenger falsely attributed speech to God, God would seize him by the hand and cut his aorta.
rows.anchor: فكأنه تعالى قال: لو كذب علينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking someone by the forelock means seizing, raising, and humiliating its owner; the forelock stands for the person.
rows.anchor: أي لنأخذن بها، ثم لنقيمنه ولنذلنه إما في الدنيا وإما في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condemned are dragged toward Hell by their forelocks and feet; the forelock phrase denotes the person who bears it.
rows.anchor: ثم قال: ناصية كاذبة خاطئة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan takes باليمين as بالميامن and, like the idiomatic reading, understands the threat to end in cutting the aorta, the heart’s vital vein.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا المعنى ذهب الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dariʿ is a Hijaz plant whose fresh growth is called shibriq; it does not fatten or satisfy, as Imruʾ al-Qays’s cited verse also names shibriq.
rows.anchor: والضريع: نبت يكون بالحجاز، يقال لرطبه: الشبرق، لا يسمن ولا يشبع

rows.speaker: امرؤ القيس
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays uses شبرق for the plant in a description of sandy terrain.
rows.anchor:
قال امرؤ القيس :
فأتبعتهم طرفي وقد حال دونهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He analyzes غِسلين morphologically as a فعْلين form from غسلت, as if it meant wash-water or runoff.
rows.anchor: وغسلين: فعلين من غسلت، كأنه الغسالة

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some commentators say ghislin is what flows from the bodies of the punished.
rows.anchor: قال بعض المفسرين: هو ما يسيل من أجساد المعذبين

rows.speaker: عكرمة ومن تابعه
rows.claim: Ikrima and those following him read قطر آن in place of قطران.
rows.anchor: وسرابيلهم من قطر آن قراءة عكرمة ومن تابعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qitr is copper and ān is what has reached its greatest heat; some wear pitch and others molten copper, at times in turn.
rows.anchor: والقطر: النحاس. والآن: الذي قد بلغ منتهى حره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the assumption that actual dariʿ grows in Hell or that people eat it: it is livestock fodder, and camels starve when eating it.
rows.anchor: فإنه لم يرد فيما يرى أهل النظر- والله أعلم- أن الضريع بعينه ينبت في النار، ولا أنهم يأكلونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image can mean people are fed what cannot satisfy them, or are punished by hunger as animals fed on dariʿ are.
rows.anchor: فأراد أن هؤلاء قوم يقتاتون ما لا يشبعهم، وضرب الضريع لهم مثلا. أو يعذبون بالجوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The audience understood this as they understood the image of a tree in Hell; otherwise they would have objected that fire consumes trees.
rows.anchor: ولو لم يكن كذلك لأنكروه كما أنكروا قوله: إنها شجرة تخرج في أصل الجحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reads the vision as what the Prophet saw on the Night Journey and told people; some apostatized and others gained insight, and the cursed tree is zaqqum.
rows.anchor: يعني بالرؤيا: ما رآه ليلة أسري به وأخبر عنه، فارتد لذلك قوم، وزاد الله في بصائر قوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also allows that dariʿ and zaqqum are plants of Hell or substances that fire cannot consume.
rows.anchor: وقد يكون الضريع وشجرة الزقوم: نبتين من النار، أو من جوهر لا تأكله النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell’s chains, fetters, shackles, scorpions, and snakes likewise need not be made of earthly substances; familiar names point to unseen things with different realities.
rows.anchor: فالأسماء متفقة للدلالة، والمعاني مختلفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because people are God’s dependents, feeding and providing for someone’s dependents counts as feeding and providing for that person.
rows.anchor: فمن أطعم عيال رجل ورزقهم، فقد رزقه وأطعمه، إذ كان رزقهم عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He expands ألا يسجدوا as ألا يا هؤلاء اسجدوا, supplying the vocative address.
rows.anchor: أراد: ألا يا هؤلاء اسجدوا لله

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s address to Salma’s house supplies a poetic example alongside the expanded vocative construction.
rows.anchor:
وقال الشاعر :
يا دار سلمى يا اسلمي ثم اسلمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An oath may omit its answer when later words make it clear; here the implied answer is that the dead will be resurrected, which the disbelievers deny.
rows.anchor: ومن الاختصار: القسم بلا جواب إذا كان في الكلام بعده ما يدل على الجواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath’s omitted answer is understood from the later challenge about being raised after becoming decayed bones.
rows.anchor: ولم يأت الجواب لعلم السامع به، إذ كان فيما تأخر من قوله دليل عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The supplicant is like someone stretching hands toward water to scoop it and bring it to his mouth; that action is left implicit.
rows.anchor: أراد: كباسط كفيه إلى الماء ليقبض عليه فيبلغه فاه

rows.speaker: ضابئ
rows.claim: Ḍābiʾ’s poem compares longing without fulfillment to clutching water that the fingers cannot hold; Arabs use the same expression for futile pursuit.
rows.anchor:
قال ضابىء :
فإني وإياكم وشوقا إليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In an oath, لا may be omitted: تفتؤوا means لا تزال تذكر يوسف.
rows.anchor: كقوله سبحانه: تالله تفتؤا تذكر يوسف

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s oath followed by أبرح قاعدا illustrates the omitted لا, meaning ‘I will not cease sitting.’
rows.anchor:
قال الشاعر :
فقلت يمين الله أبرح قاعدا

rows.speaker: الشاعر الآخر
rows.claim: A second unnamed poet’s oath is another example of the frequent omission of لا with an oath.
rows.anchor:
وقال آخر :
فلا وأبي دهماء زالت عزيزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means لئلا تضلوا, with لا understood before the verb.
rows.anchor: يبين الله لكم أن تضلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means that God holds the heavens and earth so they will not disappear, supplying لئلا.
rows.anchor: وإن الله يمسك السماوات والأرض أن تزولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning means ‘lest your deeds be annulled’; the negative لا is understood.
rows.anchor: كجهر بعضكم لبعض أن تحبط أعمالكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means Moses chose seventy men from among his people, with من omitted.
rows.anchor: واختار موسى قومه سبعين رجلا

rows.speaker: العجاج
rows.claim: Al-ʿAjjāj’s line اختار له الله الشجر means God chose something for him from among the trees.
rows.anchor:
وقال العجاج :
تحت الذي اختار له الله الشجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression means God gave them power for or over the land, with the preposition ل omitted.
rows.anchor: وكقوله: الذين إن مكناهم في الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He lists idioms that omit expected prepositions, including عدتك مائة, أستغفر الله ذنبي, شربت ماء, وثويت البصرة.
rows.anchor: والعرب تقول: عددتك مائة، أي عددت لك، وأستغفر الله ذنبي

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet says أستغفر الله ذنبا لست محصيه, illustrating the same construction with the object of seeking forgiveness.
rows.anchor:
قال الشاعر :
أستغفر الله ذنبا لست محصيه

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poet uses استجابه as a direct object construction: no responder answered the caller’s plea.
rows.anchor:
قال الشاعر :
وداع دعا يا من يجيب إلي الندى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مسؤولا means مسؤولا عنه, with عن omitted.
rows.anchor: وقوله جل وعز: إن العهد كان مسؤلا

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda cites the idiom لتسألن عهدي to mean ‘you will be asked about my covenant.’
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: يقال: (لتسألن عهدي) أي عن عهدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They ‘buy error’ by exchanging it for guidance; الهدى is omitted from the phrase.
rows.anchor: أراد: يشترون الضلالة بالهدى، فحذف (الهدى)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parallel wording in 2:16 makes explicit that error is bought in exchange for guidance.
rows.anchor: ومثله: أولئك الذين اشتروا الضلالة بالهدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘We left him’ means God left a good reputation for him among later generations, with ‘good praise’ understood.
rows.anchor: أي: أبقينا له ذكرا حسنا في الآخرين، كأنه قال: تركنا عليه ثناء حسنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse omits the disbelievers’ challenge about who could testify; لكن introduces God’s testimony in response to a preceding denial.
rows.anchor: فترك ذكر قولهم وأنزل: لكن الله يشهد بما أنزل إليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: لكن typically follows a negation and then affirms the contrary, evidence for the omitted challenge before God’s testimony.
rows.anchor: يدلك على هذا أن (لكن) إنما تجيء بعد نفي لشيء فيوجب ذلك الشيء بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The crow is understood to dig soil over a dead crow to show Cain how to bury his brother’s body.
rows.anchor: أراد: فبعث الله غرابا يبحث التراب على غراب ميت ليواريه، ليريه كيف يواري سوأة أخيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sincerity is required because hypocrisy is a sin of the heart and sincerity is the heart’s repentance.
rows.anchor: ثم شرط الإخلاص، لأن النفاق ذنب القلب، والإخلاص توبة القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says repentant hypocrites are with believers, not that they themselves are believers, then promises reward to believers rather than using a pronoun for them, out of aversion and distancing.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل: فأولئك هم المؤمنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording avoids referring back to the hypocrites by pronoun, expressing disgust, turning away, and isolating them from the speech.
rows.anchor: بغضا لهم، وإعراضا عنهم، وحيدا بالكلام عن ذكرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image shows hypocrites’ cowardice and their alertness to every alarm, fearing a mobilization against Islam and its people.
rows.anchor: فدل على جبنهم، واستشرافهم لكل ناعر، ومرهج على الإسلام وأهله

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet says a flying bird would be mistaken for marked cavalry calling two tribes, illustrating alarm at every sound.
rows.anchor: وأخذه الشاعر- وأنى له هذا الاختصار- فقال

rows.speaker: الشاعر الآخر
rows.claim: Another poet says the subject kept mistaking everything after them for cavalry and infantry charging, paralleling the verse’s fearful suspicion.
rows.anchor:
وقال الآخر :
ما زلت تحسب كل شيء بعدهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun’s turning away shows God’s care for the sleepers: their cave faced Banāt Naʿsh, while the sun passed behind it throughout its course.
rows.anchor: فأعلمنا أنه بوأهم كهفا في مقنأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sunlight does not enter and scorch them, overheat them, alter their color, or wear their clothes.
rows.anchor: ولا تدخل عليهم فتؤذيهم بحرها وتلفحهم بسمومها، وتغير ألوانهم، وتبلي ثيابهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: فجوة is a spacious part of the cave; its airflow and coolness relieve the cave’s stuffiness and distress.
rows.anchor: أي متسع منه- ينالهم فيه نسيم الريح وبردها، وينفي عنهم غمة الغار وكربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rebukes critics who ask what is useful in the sun’s path around the cave: the wording conveys God’s subtle protection and choice of a healthy sleeping place.
rows.anchor: وأي شيء أولى بأن يكون فائدة من هذا الخبر؟ وأي معنى ألطف مما أودع الله هذا الكلام؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The critics’ failure to see the cave verse’s subtle meaning resembles their bafflement at the abandoned well and lofty palace verse, mocked as an example of flat poetry.
rows.anchor: وليس جهلهم بما في هذه الآية من لطيف المعنى، بأعجب من هذا جهلهم بمعنى قوله

rows.speaker: رؤبة بن العجاج
rows.claim: Ruʾba’s line reverses the ordinary order, saying the earth’s color is its sky’s, since both colors are the same.
rows.anchor:
وقال رؤبة بن العجاج :
ومهمه مغبرة أرجاؤه

rows.speaker: الشاعر الآخر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s ‘coal became like its soil’ means the soil became like coal, another reversal.
rows.anchor:
وقال الآخر :
وصار الجمر مثل ترابها

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda reads the wording as ‘haste was created from the human’, meaning that haste is a human trait.
rows.anchor: أي خلق العجل من الإنسان، يعني العجلة. كذلك قال أبو عبيدة

rows.speaker: خداش بن زهير
rows.claim: Khidāsh ibn Zuhayr’s line reverses the syntax by saying spears are disobeyed with the soldiers, instead of men being resisted or pierced by spears.
rows.anchor:
كقول خداش بن زهير :
وتركب خيل لا هوادة بينها

rows.speaker: الشاعر الآخر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet reverses the wording about a wild cow and a snare by mistake.
rows.anchor:
ومنه قول الآخر :
أسلمته في دمشق كما

rows.speaker: الشاعر الآخر
rows.claim: Another poet reverses the relation between stoning and adultery; he means that stoning was prescribed for adultery.
rows.anchor:
وقال آخر :
كانت فريضة ما تقول كما

rows.speaker: بعض أصحاب اللغة
rows.claim: Some linguists take the apparent shepherd comparison as inverted: the intended comparison is to the sheep being called, not to the shepherd.
rows.anchor: وكان بعض أصحاب اللغة يذهب في قول الله تعالى: ومثل الذين كفروا كمثل الذي ينعق بما لا يسمع إلا دعاء ونداء

rows.speaker: بعض أصحاب اللغة
rows.claim: They also read the keys as weighing down the strong group that carries them.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قوله سبحانه: ما إن مفاتحه لتنوأ بالعصبة أولي القوة

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: Another interpreter reverses the construction to mean that the person’s love of wealth is intense.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر في قوله سبحانه: وإنه لحب الخير لشديد

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: Another interpreter takes the prayer to mean ‘make the righteous our leaders in good’, reversing who leads whom.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله سبحانه: واجعلنا للمتقين إماما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects imposing inversion on the Qur’an without sound grounds: poets may reverse wording by mistake, for rhyme or meter, or from poetic necessity.
rows.anchor: وهذا ما لا يجوز لأحد أن يحكم به على كتاب الله عز وجل لو لم يجد له مذهبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poet examples show that inversion occurs through mistake or poetic constraint, so poetic usage alone does not justify such an interpretation of scripture.
rows.anchor: لأن الشعراء تقلب اللفظ، وتزيل الكلام على الغلط، أو على طريق الضرورة للقافية

rows.speaker: ابن الكلبي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Kalbī says Labīd’s ‘four sons of Umm al-Banīn’ were actually five; the poet made them four to fit the rhyme.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الكلبي: هم خمسة، فجعلهم للقافية أربعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing youths circling with vessels, the text implies ‘they are served’ fruit, meat, and houris, since those are not carried around.
rows.anchor: والفاكهة واللحم والحور العين لا يطاف بها، وإنما أراد: ويؤتون بلحم طير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means ‘settle your plan and summon your partners’, with the verb ادعوا omitted before شركاءكم.
rows.anchor: فأجمعوا أمركم وشركاءكم [يونس: 71] أي: وادعوا شركاءكم

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd’s codex makes the understood verb explicit in this passage.
rows.anchor: وكذلك هو في مصحف عبد الله

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s line means ‘he cuts off his nose and gouges his eyes’, with the second verb omitted.
rows.anchor:
قال الشاعر :
تراه كأن الله يجدع أنفه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ’s verse means he fed the animal straw and gave it cold water; the verb ‘gave water’ is omitted.
rows.anchor:
وأنشد الفراء :
علفتها تبنا وماء باردا

rows.speaker: الشاعر الآخر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet means that the women kohl their eyes, with the second verb understood after ‘plucked their brows’.
rows.anchor:
وقال آخر :
إذا ما الغانيات برزن يوما

rows.speaker: الشاعر الآخر
rows.claim: Another poet’s ‘wearing a sword and spear’ means wearing the sword and carrying the spear.
rows.anchor:
وقال الآخر :
ورأيت زوجك في الوغى

words: وَلَوْ أَنَّ قُرْءَانًۭا سُيِّرَتْ بِهِ ٱلْجِبَالُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional sentence omits its answer, understood as ‘this would have been that Quran’.
rows.anchor: أراد: لكان هذا القرآن، فحذف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unstated result of ‘were it not for God’s favor and mercy’ is ‘He would have punished you’.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قوله: ولولا فضل الله عليكم

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s conditional oath likewise leaves its answer unstated: they would have refused any messenger other than you.
rows.anchor:
قال الشاعر :
فأقسم لو شيء أتانا رسوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse names one upright group from the People of the Book but leaves the contrasting group unstated, although سواء compares two or more.
rows.anchor: فذكر أمة واحدة ولم يذكر بعدها أخرى. وسواء تأتي للمعادلة بين اثنين فما زاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrasting person is omitted from the description of the night worshipper because ‘Do those who know and those who do not know become equal?’ supplies the comparison.
rows.anchor: ولم يذكر ضد هذا، لأن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated wording in these examples strengthens and emphasizes the meaning.
rows.anchor: كل هذا يراد به التأكيد للمعنى الذي كرر به اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated promise of ease is another instance of repetition for emphasis.
rows.anchor: وقال: فإن مع العسر يسرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated warning is cited as an emphatic repetition.
rows.anchor: وقال: أولى لك فأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the question about Judgment Day also emphasizes its meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال: وما أدراك ما يوم الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary speech also repeats commands for force, as in ‘hurry, hurry’ and ‘shoot, shoot’.
rows.anchor: وقد يقول القائل للرجل: اعجل اعجل، وللرامي: ارم ارم

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet repeats كم several times in a line as an emphatic expression.
rows.anchor:
وقال الشاعر :
كم نعمة كانت لكم كم كم وكم

rows.speaker: الشاعر الآخر
rows.claim: Another poet repeats the question أين أينا in a verse about Kinda’s retreat.
rows.anchor:
وقال الآخر :
هلا سألت جموع كن

rows.speaker: عوف بن الخرع
rows.claim: ʿAwf ibn al-Kharaʿ repeats أولى in his line about Fazāra to illustrate emphatic repetition.
rows.anchor:
وقال عوف بن الخرع :
وكادت فزارة تصلي بنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adjectives may vary one consonant in a repeated pair to avoid repeating the same word: عطشان نطشان, حسن بسن, شيطن ليطان.
rows.anchor: كقولهم: (عطشان نطشان) كرهوا أن يقولوا: عطشان عطشان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh urged the Prophet to worship their gods in exchange for their worshipping his God; God repeats the response to end their hopes and disabuse them.
rows.anchor: لأنهم أرادوه على أن يعبد ما يعبدون، ليعبدوا ما يعبد، وأبدؤوا في ذلك وأعادوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This refusal echoes the warning that the disbelievers wished the Prophet to compromise so they could compromise in their religion.
rows.anchor: وهو معنى قوله: ودوا لو تدهن فيدهنون

rows.speaker: زيد بن ثابت
rows.claim: Zayd reports that after Ibn Umm Maktum explained his disability, the Prophet dictated the exception غير أولي الضرر to the verse he was writing.
rows.anchor: قال زيد: فثقلت فخذ رسول الله، صلى الله عليه وسلم، على فخذي حتى خشيت أن ترضها، ثم قال: اكتب

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن أم مكتوم
rows.claim: Ibn Umm Maktum said he wished to fight in God’s cause but had the disability the Prophet could see.
rows.anchor: فجاء عبد الله ابن أم مكتوم فقال: يا رسول الله إني أحب الجهاد في سبيل الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation for repeated wording is that revelation descended gradually, sometimes only a few words or verses at a time.
rows.anchor: وفيه وجه آخر، وهو: أن القرآن كان ينزل شيئا بعد شيء وآية بعد آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle ألا may be extra, serving to call attention.
rows.anchor: و (ألا) تزاد في الكلام للتنبيه

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The poet’s line uses extra ألا and omits أن from the intended phrase ‘أيها الزاجري أن أحضر الوغى’.
rows.anchor:
وقال الشاعر :
ألا أيهذا الراجزي أحضر الوغى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition باء can be extra and omitted in the meaning; here the phrase means تنبت الدهن.
rows.anchor: والباء تزاد في الكلام، والمعنى إلقاؤها. كقوله سبحانه: تنبت بالدهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He treats the bāʾ in باسم as extra, giving the meaning ‘read the name of your Lord’.
rows.anchor: وقوله: اقرأ باسم ربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means عباد الله يشربونها, with the preposition omitted from the sense.
rows.anchor: وعينا يشرب بها عباد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction means ‘shake the palm trunk toward yourself’, treating باء as extra.
rows.anchor: وهزي إليك بجذع النخلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means أيكم المفتون, with the bāʾ omitted from the sense.
rows.anchor: فستبصر ويبصرون (5) بأيكم المفتون

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā’s line says the spears secured their dependents’ provision, using باء where the direct object is meant.
rows.anchor:
وقال الأعشى :
ضمنت برزق عيالنا أرماحنا

rows.speaker: الشاعر الآخر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s phrase نرجو بالفرج illustrates the extra preposition before a direct object.
rows.anchor:
وقال الآخر :
نضرب بالسيف ونرجو بالفرج

rows.speaker: امرؤ القيس
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays’s هصرت بغصن means ‘I bent a branch’, with باء extra.
rows.anchor:
وقال امرؤ القيس :
هصرت بغصن ذي شماريخ ميال

rows.speaker: أمية بن أبي الصلت
rows.claim: Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt uses بالدقيق where the flour is the direct object, another example of bāʾ being extra.
rows.anchor:
وقال أمية بن أبي الصلت :
إذ يسفون بالدقيق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ in the expression about offering affection to them is another example of the particle being extra.
rows.anchor: وقال: تلقون إليهم بالمودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ in the expression about intending wrongdoing at the sanctuary is another cited extra preposition.
rows.anchor: وقوله: ومن يرد فيه بإلحاد بظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: من may be extra: ما أريد منهم من رزق means ‘I do not want sustenance from them’.
rows.anchor: و (من) قد تزاد في الكلام أيضا، كقوله: ما أريد منهم من رزق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everyday ما أتاني من أحد means ما أتاني أحد, showing the same extra من.
rows.anchor: وتقول: ما أتاني من أحد، أي أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām may be extra, as in the phrase about those who fear their Lord.
rows.anchor: و (اللام) قد تزاد، كقوله سبحانه: للذين هم لربهم يرهبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kāf may be extra in the statement that nothing is like God.
rows.anchor: و (الكاف) قد تزاد، كقوله: ليس كمثله شيء

rows.speaker: حميد بن ثور
rows.claim: Ḥumayd ibn Thawr’s line means the tree pleases every branch of the acacia, treating على as extra.
rows.anchor:
قال حميد بن ثور :
أبى الله إلا أن سرحة مالك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: عن may be extra in the phrase about those who oppose the Prophet’s command.
rows.anchor: و (عن) تزاد قال تعالى: يخالفون عن أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says the emphatic particle إن الثقيلة may be extra, citing this verse and the wording about death in 62:8.
rows.anchor: و (إن الثقيلة) تزاد كقوله سبحانه: إن الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات إنا لا نضيع أجر من أحسن عملا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also cites the emphatic إن before ‘death, from which you flee’ as an instance of the particle being extra.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قوله: قل إن الموت الذي تفرون منه فإنه ملاقيكم

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s line repeats إن in a construction that Ibn Qutayba cites as an example of the emphatic particle’s extra use.
rows.anchor:
وقال الشاعر :
إن الخليفة إن الله سربله
